section_summary: The section concludes a technical list of changes to Japanese radio call signs and emergency police radio registrations, including frequencies, emissions, station locations, and corrections to an earlier July list. It then documents a diplomatic exchange concerning interference on Japan's 4495-kilocycle aircraft-control frequency from a station in North Korea. The Soviet Foreign Ministry declined to assist because the alleged source lay outside Soviet territory.

subfiles.title: Changes of Call Sign and Emergency Police Radio Lists (continuation)
subfiles.about: Lists changes and corrections to Japanese radio call signs and emergency police radio registrations.
subfiles.summary: The continuation first records changed call signs or frequencies for stations at Osaka, Hikone, and Tokyo, as well as portable or mobile operations in coastal waters. It then gives emergency police stations throughout Japan with their registration numbers, frequencies, call signs, emissions, operating restrictions, addresses, and coordinates. Heavy type denotes changes, while asterisks identify corrections to errata in the July list.

subfiles.title: Incoming Telegram No. 3176 Concerning the Soviet Reply on Radio Interference
subfiles.about: Reports the substance of the Soviet Foreign Ministry's reply concerning interference with a radio frequency used in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that a Soviet Foreign Ministry note dated December 15 states that the interfering station is outside the Soviet Union. The reply gives no indication that the Soviet authorities intend to assist in eliminating the interference, and the Embassy promises to forward the full text by despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 809: Radio Interference Experienced by Aircraft Control Tower Frequency in Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards and explains the Soviet response to a protest about North Korean interference on Japan's aircraft-control frequency.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy recalls the Department's October 4 telegram concerning interference from a North Korean station on the 4495-kilocycle aircraft-control frequency, for which the United States held a registration dating from October 27, 1938. It notes that Embassy note no. 577 asked the Soviet Foreign Ministry for assistance. Soviet note no. 83 replied only that the offending station was not within Soviet territory; a translation is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Translation of Soviet Ministry of Foreign Affairs Note No. 83
subfiles.from: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the USSR
subfiles.to: Embassy of the United States of America, Moscow
subfiles.about: Declines the American request for Soviet assistance in ending radio interference allegedly originating at Hamhung in North Korea.
subfiles.summary: The Soviet Foreign Ministry acknowledges Embassy note no. 577, which requested help in stopping interference on 4495 kilocycles allegedly caused by a station at Hamhung in North Korea. It states that the Soviet government cannot comply because the station identified by the United States is outside Soviet territory.
